big_idea: We measure with non-standard UNITS — cubes, hands, footsteps. Same object: many units.
learning_intention: We are learning to measure with non-standard units.
student_learning_goal: I can measure with cubes, hands, or footsteps.
success_criteria: I can line up cubes along an object to count its length.
I can measure with my hand-spans.
I can pick the right unit (cube, hand, footstep) for a job.
lesson_specific_materials: OPTIONAL: Max and Tess — if available; otherwise teacher voices both characters in two distinct voices, or substitutes two stuffed animals / paper-bag puppets / pictures on the anchor poster. Activity is unaffected.
Tape on the floor for footstep measuring
Lesson 4 measurement tracker — provided in assessment_suite stage

minds_on.hook: Max: My measuring stick says 5 CUBES LONG. Can YOUR pencil be 5 cubes long?
minds_on.teacher_script:
Bring children to the carpet. Max + Tess puppets. 'For 3 days we COMPARED. Today we MEASURE — count UNITS.'

Write MEASURE and UNIT on chart. 'Measure = count how many UNITS long.'

Demonstrate with cubes. Pencil + 5 linking cubes alongside, TOUCHING. 'Pencil = 5 cubes long.'

Marker = 7 cubes — longer than pencil.

Key rule. 'Cubes must TOUCH — no gaps, no overlaps. Same size cubes.'

Other units. Hand-span across a desk: '6 hands.' Heel-to-toe footsteps to door: '8 steps.'

Unit choice: 'Cubes for SMALL. Hands for MEDIUM. Footsteps for LONG.'

Max's RULE: 'LINE IT UP — COMPARE — NAME IT!' For measure: line up the units (touching), compare to a count, name the number.

Class refrain. Class chants 3x with claps: 'LINE IT UP — COMPARE — NAME IT! That's how Max measures!'

'Today we MEASURE with cubes, hands, and footsteps.'

steps.instruction: Whole group: measure 4 objects with cubes. (a) pencil. (b) marker. (c) book. (d) eraser. Compare results.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say: 'Predict how many cubes. Now measure.'

steps.instruction: Three stations. Station A: Cube Measure — pair measures 5 classroom items with linking cubes and records counts. Station B: Hand-Spans — pair measures 5 desks/tables with hand-spans. Station C: Footsteps — pair measures 5 distances (table to door, etc.) with footsteps.
Stretch challenge at Station A: measure the same object twice, once with cubes, once with hand-spans. Are they the same number?
Discuss unit choice. 'Cubes for SMALL things (pencils). Hands for MEDIUM (desks). Footsteps for LONG (rooms).' Why?
steps.teacher_prompt: Demonstrate: 'A door in cubes = 80. In footsteps = 1. Which is easier to count?'

steps.instruction: Circulate to record formative evidence on the measurement tracker.
steps.teacher_prompt: Stop at each pair. Ask 'How many cubes? Show me.' Mark the tracker.

differentiation.for_emerging: Stay at Station A. Just count cubes (skip hand and footstep stations).
differentiation.for_extending: Stretch at Station C: measure with footsteps AND with hand-spans, compare numbers; ask why one might give a bigger number than the other.
differentiation.for_ell_or_iep: Provide a sentence frame: 'My ___ is ___ cubes long.'
differentiation.for_movement_learners: NO-CUBE, NO-PAPER PATH: measure entirely with bodies and existing classroom objects. How many heel-to-toe footsteps from one wall to another? How many hand-spans across the carpet? How many pencils lined up tip-to-tip across a desk? Whole lesson can run with NO purchased linking cubes — pencils, books, hand-spans, and footsteps as same-size unit substitutes.

formative_check.what_to_look_for: Three signals: lines up cubes carefully (no gaps); counts accurately; picks an appropriate unit.

discussion_prompts: What does MEASURE mean? (Count units lined up.)
Why must cubes TOUCH? (Gaps lose count; overlaps double-count.)
When is hand-spans better than cubes? (For medium things — a desk would take too many cubes.)
When is footsteps better than hand-spans? (For long things — a room would take too many hand-spans.)
consolidation.exit_routine: Refrain chant 3x. Then each child completes the sentence frame: 'My ___ is ___ cubes long.' Sticky-note one measurement and post.

assessment_in_this_lesson.rationale: Lesson 4 captures A10.1 mastery for non-standard units.

expanded_walkthrough.title: When the child leaves GAPS between cubes — repairing the unit-iteration gap trap at K (Lehrer, 2003; Stephan & Cobb, 2003; Battista, 2007)
expanded_walkthrough.rationale:
On A10.1 measurement with non-standard units, the most-documented K trap is the unit-iteration gap trap: child lines up cubes with spaces between them or with overlaps, then counts the cubes — not the LENGTH the cubes cover. They've grasped 'count the cubes' but not yet 'cubes must TILE the length without gaps or overlaps'.

Lehrer (2003) calls this the early-iteration phase: children treat the unit as an object to be counted (cardinal use) rather than as a covering of space (measurement use). Stephan & Cobb (2003) traced classroom development and found children move from counting placed objects, to placing-then-counting, to mentally projecting unit copies along a length — but only when teachers explicitly draw attention to gap and overlap. Battista (2007) frames spatial measurement as requiring the child to coordinate 'unit' (the cube) with 'extent' (the length), and to recognise that gaps leave un-counted extent while overlaps double-count.

Why this matters: if K children leave with gaps allowed, two students measuring the same object get different numbers and lose faith in measurement as objective. The 'cubes touch — no gaps, no overlaps' move is what makes non-standard units function as units rather than counters.

The walkthrough covers the precise moment when a child leaves gaps.
expanded_walkthrough.setup: Pair is at Station A. Child measures a pencil with cubes. Cubes are spaced loosely; reports '3 cubes' for what's actually a 5-cube pencil.
expanded_walkthrough.teacher_script:
Crouch. 'You said 3 cubes. Let's CHECK — push the cubes TOGETHER. No spaces.'

Push the cubes tight against each other. 'Now count.' Child counts 5. 'See — when there are GAPS, we count too few. When cubes touch, we count right.'

Walk through. 'Max says — LINE IT UP touching. COMPARE the count to the pencil. NAME IT.'

Generalise. 'Imagine a parade — animals shoulder-to-shoulder. No empty spots. That's how cubes line up.'

Now re-measure 3 more objects with the 'no-gap' rule.

If still gapping: provide a guideline strip with cube-spaced marks. 'One cube in each box.' Force the alignment.

Long-term recovery: every measurement starts with 'cubes touching, no overlaps'.
expected_student_responses: (Confused) Leaves gaps; counts placed cubes (cardinal use), not the length they cover.
(Mid) Closes gaps with prompts; counts correctly after.
(Strong) Lines cubes tight from the start; counts independently.
(Stretched) Notices when cubes overlap and corrects without prompts; can articulate 'cubes have to cover the WHOLE length, no holes'.
common_misconceptions: Gaps don't matter — I just count the cubes I placed. (Repair: gaps are un-counted length; the length is what we're measuring.)
Overlaps don't matter. (Repair: overlapping cubes double-count the same bit of length.)
Bigger cubes give a bigger measurement. (Repair: same-size cubes only — that's what makes them 'units'.)
recovery_moves: DIAGNOSTIC A — child leaves visible gaps and counts cubes: provide a guideline strip with cube-spaced boxes drawn in pencil; one cube per box; the box visualises the LENGTH each cube must cover; do this for the next 3 measurements until the child closes gaps spontaneously.

DIAGNOSTIC B — child overlaps cubes (squeezes them in for a bigger count): hold a cube up and trace its OWN length on the table with a marker; show that overlapping makes two cubes claim the same bit of table; rule: 'each bit of length gets ONE cube, no sharing'.

DIAGNOSTIC C — child uses cubes of different sizes and counts them all the same: pre-sort cubes by colour-equals-size and rule that ONLY ONE COLOUR can be used for any one measurement; reinforce that 'unit' means 'same size every time'.

worksheet_brief.purpose: Independent practice of A10.1 measurement with non-standard units.

parts_outline.task: Look at 4 pictures. Count the cubes alongside each object. Write the number.
Pick the right unit. Match cubes / hands / footsteps to 4 objects of different sizes.
Measure 3 things at home with cubes (or any same-size objects). Draw and record counts.
